intro: Two hundred years ago, a small cut could kill you, surgery meant terrible pain, and no one knew that tiny living germs cause many diseases. Doctors blamed bad air. Then, one careful test at a time, people began to find the real causes. A country doctor tried cowpox. A London doctor mapped a neighborhood. A chemist looked at spoiled wine under a microscope.

In this unit you will follow those discoveries, from Jenner's first vaccine in 1796 to penicillin, insulin, the polio vaccine and the shape of DNA in the 1900s. You will see how clean water, sewers and safe food, including work in Chicago and Peoria, helped people live about thirty years longer.

By the end, you will be able to explain germ theory, tell how vaccines and antibiotics work and how they differ, read simple health data, and describe how scientists change their minds when the evidence is strong.
bigQuestion: How did finding the true causes of disease change medicine and help people live longer?

timeline.t: Edward Jenner tests cowpox to protect against smallpox
Ether is shown to make surgery painless in Boston
Semmelweis has doctors wash hands in Vienna
John Snow traces cholera to the Broad Street pump
Robert Koch identifies the tuberculosis germ
Pasteur's rabies vaccine saves Joseph Meister
Insulin is first used to treat a patient in Toronto
The double-helix shape of DNA is published
Salk's polio vaccine is declared safe and effective

test.q: Who first tested cowpox as protection against smallpox?
test.why: Edward Jenner tested cowpox on James Phipps in 1796.
Miasma was the old belief that bad air caused disease; germ theory replaced it.

test.q: What did John Snow's 1854 map point to?
choices: A water pump on Broad Street
test.why: Snow's map showed cholera deaths clustered around the Broad Street pump.

choices: Doctors washing their hands saved mothers' lives
test.why: Handwashing with chlorine solution sharply cut deaths in his clinic.

test.q: Which scientist gave the first rabies vaccine to a bitten boy in 1885?
test.why: Pasteur's team treated Joseph Meister in 1885.

test.q: What did Robert Koch identify in 1882?
test.why: Koch announced the tuberculosis bacterium in 1882.

test.q: How did Lister's antiseptic surgery work?
choices: It put patients to sleep with ether
It used X-rays to see inside
It used carbolic acid to kill germs in wounds and on tools
test.why: Lister used carbolic acid to kill germs, which cut deaths from infection.

test.q: What was demonstrated at the Ether Dome in 1846?
test.why: Ether was shown to let a patient sleep through surgery without real pain.
Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop their growth; they do not work on viruses.

test.q: Why was a lab in Peoria, Illinois, important?
choices: It found the cause of cholera
It helped mass-produce penicillin during World War II
test.why: The Peoria lab grew penicillin mold in tanks and found a high-yield mold.

test.q: Which statement about insulin is accurate?
choices: It cures diabetes in one dose
It is a daily treatment that lets people with type 1 diabetes live full lives
test.why: Insulin manages type 1 diabetes but does not cure it.

test.q: What was the result of the 1954 polio field trial, announced in 1955?
choices: Salk's vaccine was safe and worked
test.why: On April 12, 1955, the vaccine was declared safe and effective.

test.q: How did Rosalind Franklin contribute to the discovery of DNA's shape?
choices: Her X-ray photo of DNA showed key clues
test.why: Franklin's Photo 51 helped Watson and Crick work out the double helix.

test.q: Why did U.S. life expectancy rise so much in the 1900s?
choices: Mostly because far fewer children died of infections
test.why: Clean water, safe food, vaccines and antibiotics meant far fewer children died young.

test.q: Which is an example of public health work?
test.why: Public health protects whole communities, like treating water for everyone.

write.prompt: Which did more to help people live longer in the 1800s and 1900s: new medicines such as vaccines and antibiotics, or public health work such as clean water and safe food? Make a claim and support it with two or three facts or sources from this unit.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence.
Name your evidence, such as Snow's map, the life expectancy table or the polio case numbers.
Give the other side fairly before you explain why your side is stronger.
Use unit terms such as public health, vaccine and antibiotic.
